summary:
Selene Temple is a web platform that compares candidate landing sites at the lunar south pole (Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge). For each site it shows where the Sun and the Earth are, hour by hour, against that site's real terrain horizon, computed from NASA LOLA elevation data and JPL Horizons ephemerides. That answers two questions that decide whether a lander can live there: when does the site get sunlight for solar power, and when does it have a direct line of sight to Earth for communication?
The same calculations power two modes. Educational mode starts on a 3D Moon with the Apollo landing sites, NASA photos and simple charts anyone can read, and rates any point you click as good or bad to land. Expert mode shows time series, horizon profiles, parameters, the exact JPL Horizons query and data download. Every number shows its origin, and missing data is shown as "no data", never invented. Available in English and Portuguese.
details:
Selene Temple (Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge) compares candidate landing sites at the lunar south pole by checking, hour by hour, when the Sun and the Earth are above each site's real terrain horizon. The name comes from Selene, the Greek Titaness who personifies the Moon.

THE PROBLEM. At the south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so terrain decides everything: a crater rim can be lit for long periods while a site a few kilometres away is in shadow. The Earth also hangs near the horizon and a ridge can cut the radio link. Choosing a site means comparing how much of the time the Sun (solar power) and the Earth (communication) are visible. As lunar missions advance, a human presence on the Moon will become real again, and society will need to be educated about it more and more. That is why Educational mode exists, and why it is built around the Apollo landings: the first human footprints on the Moon are the best starting point to explain why landing sites matter today.

WHAT IT DOES.

- Educational mode opens on a 3D Moon (NASA CGI Moon Kit + LROC detail) with the nine Artemis III candidate regions, their outlines, names and a red border at 80°S. Six Apollo landing sites open a window with up to 100 official NASA images, a history text, a Wikipedia link and study questions. Simple charts and a "good or bad to land" explanation are written for students.

- Expert mode shows a flat south polar map, margin charts, the horizon panorama with the Sun and Earth paths, all parameters, links that reproduce each JPL Horizons query, region comparison (including charts) and CSV/JSON download. Percentages are also shown as equivalent hours of the one-month forecast.

- Clicking any point south of 80°S computes it on demand (when the local API runs) and can be saved to Favorites.

- A guided tour, English and Portuguese, and five text sizes.

HOW IT WORKS. The terrain horizon is built from the NASA LOLA 20 m elevation model: for each azimuth (1° steps) the code scans outward up to 150 km, including lunar curvature (radius 1737.4 km), and keeps the highest angle. Sun and Earth positions seen from the site come from the JPL Horizons API (observer 2 m above ground). A body counts as visible when the centre of its disc is above the horizon. Region results are pre-computed, so the published site works without any live service. Every number shows its origin (observed, model, estimate or no data); missing data is never invented.

VALIDATION. For Malapert Massif (2026-11-15 to 2026-12-15) all 31 Sun rows match JPL Horizons to the sixth decimal and all 31 Earth rows within 0.0005°. The horizon calculation was also tested against analytic cases. Details: docs/validation.md in the repository.

HONEST LIMITS. One 30-day period (January 2027); region markers are centres of the USGS grids, not selected landing points; elevation data ends at 80°S; visibility uses the disc centre. Not a mission certification tool.

TOOLS. Vite + TypeScript, Leaflet, Three.js, FastAPI, Python (NumPy, rasterio). Source code: https://github.com/Kaykyduken/Projeto-de-site-de-explora-o-lunar

Independent hackathon project. Not an official NASA product and not endorsed by NASA.
